1.pericope_label: And I turned, and lifted up mine eyes, and looked, and, behold, there came four chariots out from between two mountains; and the mountains were mountains of brass. In the first chariot were red horses; and in the second chariot black horses; And in the third chariot white horses; and in the fourth chariot grisled and bay horses
debates: Whether the four chariots are four empires or providence in general
What the mountains of brass stand for
Whether the fourth chariot has one colour of horses or two
outliers: Calvin calls the reading that finds the four Gospels here a very frigid view
Ellicott would emend the fourth colour by conjecture from the Syriac
Henry confesses himself very much in the dark about the whole vision
themes: Chariots driving out from a pass between two hills
Mountains of brass that cannot be moved
Horses clothed in red like flaming torches
A white horse led in a triumph

4.pericope_label: Then I answered and said unto the angel that talked with me, What are these, my lord? And the angel answered and said unto me, These are the four spirits of the heavens, which go forth from standing before the Lord of all the earth. The black horses which are therein go forth into the north country
debates: Whether the four are spirits, winds or angels
Which empire each colour of horse stands for
Whether the colours carry a fixed meaning at all
outliers: Ellicott denies that the colours may be read out of the Book of Revelation
Ellicott finds the interpreting angel giving way to the prophet in mid-sentence
Gill offers the Huns, Goths and Vandals for the horses that seek leave to go
themes: Chariots sent out to the four quarters
A country always spoken of as the north
Horses asking leave before they run
Wrath quieted rather than a spirit put to rest

9.pericope_label: And the word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Take of them of the captivity, even of Heldai, of Tobijah, and of Jedaiah, which are come from Babylon, and come thou the same day, and go into the house of Josiah the son of Zephaniah; Then take silver and gold, and make crowns, and set them upon the head of Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest
debates: Whether the visitors had returned for good or were only visiting
Whether one crown was made or two
Why the crown goes to the priest and not to the governor
outliers: Ellicott explains the changed names by the common use of several names for one person
Clarke counts the manuscripts that read a single crown
Henry faults the visitors for not having settled in their own land
themes: A sign done in the open where a vision was private
Silver and gold carried up from Babylon
A crown that is not a mitre
A throne left empty on purpose

12.pericope_label: And speak unto him, saying, Thus speaketh the Lord of hosts, saying, Behold the man whose name is The BRANCH; and he shall grow up out of his place, and he shall build the temple of the Lord: Even he shall build the temple of the Lord; and he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule upon his throne; and he shall be a priest upon his throne: and the counsel of peace shall be between them both
debates: Whether the Branch is the governor or the Messiah
Whether priest here may be softened to prince and throne to seat
Who the two are between whom the counsel of peace stands
outliers: Ellicott argues from the silence about the governor that the hearers must have looked higher
Ellicott rejects four readings of the counsel of peace before offering his own
Clarke reports that the Chaldee renders the name outright as my Messiah
themes: A branch growing out of its own place
A crown worn where a mitre belongs
A priest seated instead of standing
A council held between two who are one

14.pericope_label: And the crowns shall be to Helem, and to Tobijah, and to Jedaiah, and to Hen the son of Zephaniah, for a memorial in the temple of the Lord. And they that are far off shall come and build in the temple of the Lord, and ye shall know that the Lord of hosts hath sent me unto you
debates: Whether one crown was laid up or two
What the crowns are a memorial of
Whether the closing sentence is complete as it stands
outliers: Ellicott concludes that the end of the passage has simply been lost
Clarke reports a reading in which the crowns become praise
Gill lists nine respects in which the Gentiles were afar off
themes: A crown hung up where it can be seen
Men remembered only by their names
Living stones carried in from a distance
A sentence that stops before its end
